name: Zane Dubois

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to employers, AI firms, unions or government. Your answers stay confidential. What does a normal workday look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead a timber-framing crew on apartment building sites, checking the wall panels, the lifting points and the fixings before the next floor goes up. My vocational trade certificate taught me the rules; years of watching a panel swing taught me when to stop a lift. I sometimes use AI to tidy an order email, then check the numbers against the drawing. My partner and I have grown children, pay above the usual rate, more than six months of expenses saved and several builders hiring nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my crew that if AI only speeds the office, fine; the wall panel still has to fit. I use it for an occasional email, not for a lift plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My wages and savings are sound enough to handle a modest change. I would watch for a wrong panel count because a machine-written order can sound confident even when it misses a balcony opening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep leading the panel lifts and check every order against the site drawing. In the first year I would show the apprentice the lift-point marks and use the same occasional AI drafting help for routine emails.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. I like a quicker answer from the office if the right wall arrives on the truck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a wrong count cost?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A whole morning if the missing panel has to be cut elsewhere. We would still have to pay for the crane while it waited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you teach before a lift?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The apprentice points out the lifting eyes and the exclusion area where nobody stands under the load. Then I check the pins myself.

say: **Office AI** may speed emails without replacing site panel lifts.
A **wall panel** still needs measuring before it is ordered.
think: Our **high wages** and savings make a minor change manageable.
A confident **AI order** might still omit a balcony opening.
do: **Keep** leading panel lifts and checking orders against drawings.
**Show** the apprentice lift points and exclusion areas before work.
feel: **Calm** if the office becomes a little quicker.
S0.quote: I like a quicker answer from the office if the right wall arrives on the truck.
fieldNote: His **occasional AI use** is limited to writing emails, with counts checked against drawings.
Strong **savings** and many local employers make a modest office change feel safe.

steps.text: Keep leading panel lifts and verify orders against site drawings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the site manager that an AI schedule should leave time for a safe panel lift. I would try a planner after another crew has shown it handles crane access and weather delays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The office may change quickly, but most of my day remains on site with timber and steel fixings. If management tries to squeeze our lift time, I have other local builders and enough savings to refuse an unsafe timetable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask to see the planner on a completed building and compare its lift times with our records. If an actual funded class place opens during paid hours, I would learn its crane and access functions in the first year, then keep a manual safety check before each lift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about shortcuts, though not about my own pay. A screen can say ready while the wind says otherwise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the planner credible?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It needs to show the crane setup time, the access route and the wind stop written into our old records. I would watch another crew use it through a full lift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave this builder over a bad schedule?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would first put the unsafe timing in writing. If the builder kept pressing, I would apply for a posted local framing job only if its safety rules and pay cover the same standard of living.

say: **AI schedules** must allow for crane access and weather.
I would try a **planner** after another crew proves it works.
think: Hands-on **panel work** remains most of my day.
Savings and many **local builders** let me reject unsafe timetables.
do: **Compare** the planner with completed lift records.
**Learn** crane and access functions if a funded paid-time class place opens.
**Apply** for posted local framing work if unsafe pressure persists and pay holds.
feel: **Uneasy** about shortcuts, with income reasonably secure.
S1.quote: A screen can say ready while the wind says otherwise.
fieldNote: He is **steady** with new tools: he wants another crew’s full lift as proof.
His **class and fallback job** have separate triggers and require paid training or a safe, well-paid local posting.

steps.text: Take funded AI planner class if actual paid-time place opens
Apply for posted local framing job if unsafe pressure persists, safety holds and pay covers bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the gang that AGI could do the drawings and orders by 2028, but robots that lift and fix panels like people follow around 2031. I would want a paid site trial before anybody stands near a machine-held wall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My present job might last through the three-year gap, yet a 2031 robot could take panel work I expected to keep doing. We have more than six months saved and many local builders, but a wage cut would still change when my partner and I can stop working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for a paid robot-panel trial with the site safety lead and a funded, paid-time inspection course. If a real course place opens, I would take it; in the first year after 2028 I would apply for a posted local panel-inspection role only if qualified and its hours and pay cover our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the short clock, but ready to check a machine against a real lift. I have no interest in trading a safe panel crew for a robot sales video.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the trial need to show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The robot must hold a panel steady while a human checks the anchor fixings and keeps people outside the load zone. The site lead has to be able to stop the lift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the builder offers a talk, but no paid trial slot?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would listen and keep leading ordinary lifts. I would ask for a dated paid slot and safety sign-off before calling it a trial.

say: **2028 AGI** changes drawings before capable panel robots around 2031.
A **paid site trial** needs human checks and stop authority.
think: A **2031 robot** could reduce panel work I planned to keep doing.
Our **strong cushion** helps, but a wage loss still changes retirement timing.
do: **Request** a paid robot-panel trial with site safety approval.
**Take** funded inspection training if an actual paid-time place opens.
**Apply** for posted local panel-inspection work if qualified and pay covers bills.
feel: **Anxious** about a short clock, with resources to act.
S2.quote: I have no interest in trading a safe panel crew for a robot sales video.
fieldNote: The **paid trial** is requested, not scheduled or completed.
His **course and role** need a real funded place, qualification and a posted local bill-covering opening.

steps.text: Take funded robot-panel inspection course if actual paid-time place opens
Apply for posted local panel-inspection role if qualified and hours/pay cover bills
Request paid supervised robot trial with human fixing checks and stop authority

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that five years lets builders run more than a showroom test before robots reach panel work around 2034. A trained inspector should still check every anchor before the wall is closed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could learn inspection while keeping my current wages, and a few builders nearby already hire people who know panels. Retirement could be closer by then, but my partner and I need actual cost and income figures before choosing a date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep leading lifts and ask for a funded robot-inspection course with a real paid-time place and site practice. If it opens, I would complete it before 2034; in the first year after 2031 I would apply for a posted local panel-inspection job only if qualified and its wage and hours cover our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about trusting a robot too soon, but able to plan. A five-year lead is enough to test a robot’s panel fixing, not enough to excuse a bad one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What practical work would you require in the course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Checking a full-height panel’s anchors, lifting points and temporary braces on site. I would want a qualified supervisor present when the machine moves it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the inspection pay is below your current rate?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare the offer with our household bills and savings plan. If it leaves us short each month, I would keep framing or apply for another posted local role.

say: **2031 AGI** allows site trials before capable panel robots around 2034.
A trained **inspector** should check anchors before walls close.
think: I could gain **inspection skills** while current wages continue.
Retirement still needs **household figures**, not a date guessed from a card.
do: **Keep** leading lifts while seeking a funded course place.
**Complete** robot inspection training if an actual paid-time site place opens.
**Apply** for posted local panel-inspection work if qualified and pay covers bills.
feel: **Uneasy** about machine safety, with planning time.
S3.quote: A five-year lead is enough to test a robot’s panel fixing, not enough to excuse a bad one.
fieldNote: His **training plan** requires real site practice, paid hours and an actual funded place.
He separates **inspection application** from another local search if the offered wage would leave monthly bills short.

steps.text: Keep leading paid panel lifts while training terms are settled
Complete funded robot inspection course if actual paid-time site place opens
Apply for posted local panel-inspection role if qualified and hours/pay cover bills
Apply for other posted local framing work if inspection pay falls short

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the apprentices they can learn panel fixing and robot checking in a decade. AGI might change drawings by 2036, while capable site robots follow around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I may leave heavy lifts before a 2039 robot is ready, but that depends on our health, bills and dependable income. If we still need wages after 2036, I would use my certificate and site experience to find a less physical post nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep leading the crew while the lifts suit me and review retirement costs with my partner each year. If wages are still needed after 2036, I would take a funded, paid-time inspection course only if a real place opens; once qualified, I would apply for a posted local inspection or apprentice-training role only if its hours and pay cover our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the long timetable, with plenty to decide at home. A 2039 panel robot is a future question; the household budget is a present one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you leave lifts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A budget showing we can meet ordinary costs without my site wage, or a real local role with safer physical demands and enough pay. I will not choose based on my age alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you accept an unpaid training week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. If a builder wants qualified people to inspect machines, the place should be funded and the course days paid. I would keep my current shifts otherwise.

say: **2036 AGI** changes drawings before capable panel robots around 2039.
Apprentices can learn **panel fixing** and future machine checks.
think: Leaving heavy lifts depends on **income, bills** and health.
If pay is still needed, **local roles** may offer less physical work.
do: **Keep** leading lifts and review retirement costs yearly.
**Take** funded inspection training if wages needed and an actual paid-time place opens.
**Apply** for posted local inspection or training work if qualified and pay covers bills.
feel: **Calm** about the long timetable, while reviewing home finances.
S4.quote: A 2039 panel robot is a future question; the household budget is a present one.
fieldNote: His **strong cushion** and plentiful nearby jobs permit a gradual choice about physical work.
Post-2036 **training and application** depend on wage need, a funded paid-time place and a posted local bill-covering role.

steps.text: Keep panel lifts while reviewing retirement affordability annually
Take funded inspection course if wages needed and actual paid-time place opens
Apply for posted local inspection or training role if wages needed, qualified and hours/pay cover bills

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because robot panel work could arrive before crews have inspected it properly. A paid site trial with a human stop rule, funded course place and posted local inspection work at enough pay would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: When the wall is hanging from a crane, someone has to own the decision to stop the lift. A machine cannot carry that responsibility for my crew.

portrait: **Zane Dubois**, 58, leads timber-panel framing on apartment building sites and holds a vocational trade certificate.
He and his **partner** have grown children, high pay, more than six months saved and many nearby building jobs.
He uses **AI occasionally** for emails and checks the numbers before orders or lifts.
He accepts **proven tools**, seeking paid trials and funded inspection training if capable robots approach.
His **retirement choice** depends on household costs and income, with local work available if wages remain needed.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** gives the shortest time before capable robots might change panel work and crew safety.
whatWouldHelp: A real **paid trial**, funded course place and posted local bill-covering inspection role would make a safer transition.
headlineQuote: When the wall is hanging from a crane, someone has to own the decision to stop the lift.
